entries_new.name: FARC's Caguán zone
aka: San Vicente del Caguán safe haven
entries_new.founder: FARC, by grant of President Andrés Pastrana
entries_new.mechanism: A government granted the guerrillas a demilitarised area during peace talks, then took it back by force when talks ended.
entries_new.story:
The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), a Marxist-Leninist guerrilla group fighting since 1964, was handed a 42,000 square kilometre safe haven by President Andrés Pastrana on 7 November 1998, centred on the town of San Vicente del Caguán, as a confidence-building step for peace talks.
In 2001 Human Rights Watch said FARC had abducted and executed civilians in the zone it accused of helping paramilitaries, without legal defence. After an aircraft hijacking, attacks on towns and kidnappings, Pastrana ended the talks on 21 February 2002 and ordered the army to retake the zone.

entries_new.name: Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, 1996 to 2001
entries_new.stopped_by: Northern Alliance and the United States
entries_new.laws: Sharia as read by the Taliban, Hanafi school, plus Mullah Omar's edicts
entries_new.challenge: Northern Alliance; United States after September 2001
entries_new.recognition: Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates, later withdrawn
entries_new.mechanism: A militia conquered most of a country and ran its courts and law from a provincial base.
entries_new.story:
The Taliban, a militia that first appeared near Kandahar in 1994 with a reported 250,000 US dollars from local businessmen, captured Kabul in 1996 and ran the country as an Islamic emirate. By the end of 2000 it held about 90% of Afghanistan; the Northern Alliance held the northeast and kept broad international recognition.
The government applied its reading of Sharia and the edicts of Mullah Omar and held no elections. Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates withdrew recognition after the 11 September attacks, and the emirate fell on 7 December 2001. The group returned to power in 2021.

entries_new.name: Houthi-held Yemen
entries_new.challenge: Saudi-led coalition; internationally recognised Yemeni government
entries_new.mechanism: An armed movement took the capital and the state offices in it, and rules from them without recognition as Yemen's government.
entries_new.story:
The Houthis, officially Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi Shia movement from Saada in northern Yemen, backed by Iran. By May 2012 they were reported to control most of Saada, Al Jawf and Hajjah governorates. In late 2014, with help from former president Saleh, they took the capital, and on 6 February 2015 they dissolved parliament and named their Revolutionary Committee the acting authority.
A Saudi-led intervention followed to restore the internationally recognised government. A list of rebel-held areas puts Houthi territory at most of former North Yemen and parts of South Yemen, run through a body called the Supreme Political Council. Several countries designate the group as terrorist.

entries_new.name: Hamas administration in Gaza
entries_new.stopped_by: Gaza peace plan after the Israel-Hamas war
entries_new.mechanism: An elected party took one territory by force from its rival and ran a separate government there under blockade.
entries_new.story:
Hamas, a Palestinian Islamist movement with an armed wing, won a majority in the 2006 Palestinian legislative election. In June 2007 it defeated its rival Fatah in fighting in Gaza and from then on governed the Gaza Strip separately from the Palestinian Authority, while being pushed out of government posts in the West Bank. Israel and Egypt imposed an economic blockade.
Many countries and organisations have criticised its rule for human rights violations. After the war that followed its attack on Israel of 7 October 2023, Hamas announced on 6 July 2026 that its civil administration was resigning under the Gaza peace plan. A Wikipedia list of rebel-held areas still shows it holding parts of the Gaza Strip.

entries_new.name: Al-Shabaab areas of Somalia
entries_new.founder: Youth militia of the Islamic Courts Union
entries_new.challenge: Federal Government of Somalia; African Union forces; Ethiopia
entries_new.mechanism: An insurgent group runs tax, court and police departments across rural districts the federal government cannot reach.
entries_new.story:
Al-Shabaab began as a youth militia inside the Islamic Courts Union, an alliance that gave de facto government across much of Somalia until Ethiopia invaded in December 2006. It is al-Qaeda's Somali branch and calls its land the Islamic Wilayat of Somalia, which the federal government rejects.
It holds a broken network of mainly rural areas in the south and centre, with its headquarters listed at Jilib. It runs departments for taxation (Zakat), local administration (Wilayah), Islamic courts (Garsoor), police (Jaysh al-Hisbah) and intelligence. An African Union and Somali government coalition took Mogadishu and much other land from it between 2011 and 2013.

entries_new.name: Boko Haram territory in Borno
entries_new.founder: Mohammed Yusuf; Abubakar Shekau led the territorial period
entries_new.stopped_by: Nigerian army and the 2015 West African offensive
entries_new.mechanism: The group seized towns and declared them part of a caliphate.
entries_new.story:
Boko Haram, a jihadist group from northeastern Nigeria founded by Mohammed Yusuf in 2002, changed strategy in August 2014, when it overran the border town of Gwoza and its leader Abubakar Shekau announced by video that the town was part of an Islamic caliphate. Bama and other towns followed.
By January 2015 the land it held was estimated at 50,000 square kilometres in and around Borno State, though not the state capital Maiduguri. A regional offensive in 2015 took most of this back, and Nigeria's army recaptured Gwoza on 27 March. Smaller holdings in Borno and Kaduna remain listed.

entries_new.name: RUF diamond areas of Sierra Leone
entries_new.challenge: Government of Sierra Leone; West African force; UN
entries_new.cost: War estimated to have cost about 200,000 lives
entries_new.mechanism: Rebels financed a war by holding diamond fields and selling the stones.
entries_new.story:
The Revolutionary United Front (RUF), a rebel group formed by Foday Sankoh with help from Charles Taylor, fought Sierra Leone's government from 1991. It promised free schooling and a fair share of diamond money. Sankoh instead used diamond revenue to buy arms, and the group focused on guarding the mines it held, using child soldiers among the guards. It became known for cutting off civilians' limbs.
On 5 July 2000 the UN Security Council banned rough diamond imports from Sierra Leone, citing the role of the trade in the war. British and other forces weakened the group by 2001. Senior leaders were convicted of war crimes in February 2009.
entries_new.anchor: Sierra Leone, centre of the country (source gives no mine location)

entries_new.name: Shwe Kokko and Yatai New City
entries_new.founder: Kayin Border Guard Force and Yatai International Holdings Group
entries_new.challenge: Myanmar military; 2020 government tribunal; Thailand cut power and fuel in 2025; China
entries_new.mechanism: A militia on a remote border sold protection and land rights to casino and scam operators and taxed the business.
entries_new.story:
Shwe Kokko is a town in Myanmar's Kayin State, on the river border with Thailand, and the headquarters of the Kayin Border Guard Force led by Saw Chit Thu, a militia of about 6,000 troops formally under the army since 2010. A company it owns was due 30% of the profits of Yatai New City, a casino and housing project promoted as a 15 billion US dollar special economic zone by Yatai, a firm owned by She Zhijiang.
Myanmar had approved 59 villas on 22.5 acres and never approved a zone. A 2020 government tribunal halted work, and the 2021 coup let it resume. Scam centres there held trafficked workers. The force later broke with the army, renamed itself the Karen National Army and taxed gambling and scam businesses. The army raided the town on 18 November 2025 and detained 346 foreigners. The force denies involvement.

sources.t: AP via News4Jax: Myanmar military raids second scam center

entries_new.name: KK Park
entries_new.pop: A US Institute of Peace representative put scam workers at 20,000 or more in KK Park and a similar park in Shwe Kokko, July 2023
entries_new.challenge: Myanmar military; Thailand; China; ASEAN and UNODC
entries_new.mechanism: A private compound sat in a border area with only loose government control, with armed men present and workers held inside.
entries_new.story:
KK Park is a walled scam complex beside the Moei River in Myawaddy Township, Myanmar, built between 2019 and 2021 and first described as a border trade site. It held its own supermarkets, hospital, restaurants and hotels. A 2024 Deutsche Welle investigation reported 17-hour days, confiscated passports, torture and threats of murder, and victims could leave only by paying a contract termination fee.
The Myanmar military accused Karen National Union leaders of involvement because of reported land deals; the union denies it. Thailand cut its power supply in June 2023. In October 2025 the army said it had captured the park, detaining 2,198 people and seizing 30 Starlink satellite internet terminals.

entries_new.name: Kokang under the MNDAA
entries_new.currency: Renminbi used as a parallel currency
entries_new.challenge: Myanmar military; China over scam centres
entries_new.mechanism: An armed group traded a ceasefire for a self-run special region living on opium, then casinos and cross-border trade.
entries_new.story:
Kokang is a strip of about 1,895 square kilometres in Myanmar's northern Shan State, on the Chinese border, long dependent on opium. Peng Jiasheng's Communist unit held it from 1968. When the Communist Party of Burma collapsed in 1989 his force became the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and a ceasefire made Kokang an autonomous special region. It used the Chinese yuan as a parallel currency, and later ran casinos.
The army drove the MNDAA out in 2009 after it refused to become a border guard unit, with up to 30,000 refugees entering China. It retook the capital, Laukkai, in December 2023. In September 2025 China sentenced 16 members of the Ming family, a Kokang-based crime syndicate, to death over scam factories.

entries_new.name: The Warlord Era in China
entries_new.challenge: Nationalist government at Guangzhou, then Nanjing
entries_new.mechanism: Army commanders held provinces with their own troops and fought over the national capital.
entries_new.story:
After China's president Yuan Shikai died on 6 June 1916, control of the country split among rival military cliques. The Zhili clique held northern provinces, the Anhui clique held southeastern ones and Zhang Zuolin's Fengtian clique held Manchuria. Sichuan, Yunnan, Hunan and Guangxi had cliques of their own. Whoever held Beijing claimed the national government, and that claim changed hands through a run of wars and coups.
The Nationalists' Northern Expedition and the 29 December 1928 submission of Zhang's son reunified China on paper, but men such as Yan Xishan of Shanxi rebelled in 1929 and 1930 and several warlords kept influence into the 1940s.
entries_new.anchor: Beijing, seat of the contested national government

entries_new.name: Comando Vermelho in Rio de Janeiro
entries_new.mechanism: A prison gang took over neighbourhoods as the base for retail drug sales and kept out police and rivals by force.
entries_new.story:
Comando Vermelho (Red Command) is a Brazilian criminal organisation formed in 1979 in a prison on Ilha Grande, as an alliance between ordinary convicts and left-wing guerrillas jailed under the military dictatorship. In the 1980s it moved into Rio's favelas (informal hillside neighbourhoods) and the cocaine trade, and by 1986 it controlled about 70% of that trade in the favelas.
A 2020 study of 37,883 tip-line reports gave it 11.4% of Rio city's territory. From 2008 the state placed permanent police units in favelas under a policy called Pacification. It has since expanded to other states and neighbouring countries.
entries_new.anchor: Favelas of northern Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

sources.t: Correio Braziliense: Militias control 57% of Rio, study says (2020)

entries_new.name: Rio de Janeiro militias
entries_new.pop: About 2.2 million residents (12.7% of the city)
entries_new.mechanism: Armed groups hold neighbourhoods inside a working city without any claim to independence.
entries_new.story:
Milícias are armed groups in Rio de Janeiro. A study published in 2020 by researchers at Fluminense Federal University, the Fogo Cruzado data lab, the University of São Paulo's violence centre and others, built from 37,883 reports to a police tip line, found they controlled 57.5% of the city's territory, 686.75 square kilometres, and 25.5% of its neighbourhoods, home to about 2.2 million people.
The drug factions held far less land: Comando Vermelho 11.4%, Terceiro Comando 3.7%, Amigos dos Amigos 0.3%. About a quarter of the city's territory was contested, and 41.4% of residents lived in those areas.
entries_new.anchor: West Zone, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (approximate, source gives city-level figures)

entries_new.name: Oficina de Envigado in Medellín
entries_new.challenge: Colombian authorities; Clan del Golfo (Usuga Clan)
entries_new.mechanism: A criminal group acted as a private court and enforcer in drug disputes across one city and its valley.
entries_new.story:
La Oficina de Envigado (The Office of Envigado) is a Colombian criminal group founded as the debt-collecting and enforcement arm of Pablo Escobar's Medellín Cartel by Diego Murillo, known as Don Berna, who later turned on Escobar. It held extortion, gambling and money laundering across the Aburrá Valley around Medellín, and acted as chief mediator and debt collector in drug disputes.
After the AUC paramilitaries demobilised in 2005, Murillo was arrested for a politician's murder, ran the group from prison and made a deal with authorities to keep violence down. He was extradited in 2008, and rival factions then fought.

entries_new.name: Knights Templar Cartel in Michoacán
entries_new.stopped_by: Mexican federal police; civilian militias; rival cartels
entries_new.mechanism: A cartel held a Mexican state by force and fought both rivals and armed residents.
entries_new.story:
The Knights Templar Cartel was a Mexican criminal group formed by leaders who split from La Familia Michoacana after the reported death of Nazario Moreno on 9 December 2010. It took over La Familia's operations in Michoacán, Guerrero, the state of Mexico and Morelos, and taught recruits to fight and die for it.
It fought the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and civilian militias formed to clear it from Michoacán. Federal police arrested its leader Servando Gómez in February 2015 and seized many properties. It is believed to have ceased to exist by September 2017, after its last leader was reportedly killed.

entries_new.name: Mogadishu warlords
entries_new.founder: Mohamed Farah Aidid; Ali Mahdi Mohamed
entries_new.challenge: UN operations; Islamic Courts Union; Ethiopia
entries_new.mechanism: Faction commanders held parts of a capital with no central government.
entries_new.story:
Clan-based armed groups overthrew Somalia's Barre government in 1991. In the south, commanders Mohamed Farah Aidid and Ali Mahdi Mohamed, both of the United Somali Congress, fought for the capital from 17 November 1991, and a ceasefire came after four months of heavy fighting in 1992.
A UN operation clashed with Aidid's Somali National Alliance and then withdrew. Afterwards neighbourhood Islamic Courts and regional governments such as Puntland formed. Ethiopian troops invaded in 2006 to remove the Islamic Courts Union.

entries_new.name: Shining Path in Peru
entries_new.stopped_by: Capture of its leaders in 1992, 1999 and 2012
entries_new.cost: Commission estimate: 31,331 deaths or disappearances attributed to the group
entries_new.mechanism: A guerrilla party tried to replace the state through rural war, and its remnants still hold out in one valley region.
entries_new.story:
The Shining Path, officially the Communist Party of Peru, is a Maoist guerrilla group that began a "people's war" in 1980 by burning ballot boxes in the town of Chuschi on the eve of elections, aiming to replace the government. The army organised peasants into anti-rebel militias called rondas.
Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2003 that 69,280 people died or disappeared between 1980 and 2000, and estimated the Shining Path responsible for 46%. Founder Abimael Guzmán was captured in 1992. The main remaining faction operates in the VRAEM river valley region, and in 2018 distanced itself from the group's legacy to keep the support of peasants it had persecuted.

entries_new.name: UNITA at Jamba
aka: National Union for the Total Independence of Angola
entries_new.challenge: MPLA government of Angola; UN sanctions
entries_new.mechanism: A rebel movement held a remote base and diamond fields with foreign backing and ran a government in them.
entries_new.story:
UNITA, an Angolan independence movement founded in 1966, fought the ruling MPLA in the civil war from 1975 to 2002, with aid from the United States and apartheid South Africa. It based itself at Jamba in the southeastern province of Cuando Cubango, ran its own government with a chief of staff, and held much of the central highlands, including the Bié Plateau.
Diamond mines along the Cuango River funded it until 1996. A UN-commissioned report on its diamond sales led to more sanctions and fed into the Kimberley Process, the certificate scheme for rough diamonds. Its leader Jonas Savimbi was killed in an ambush on 22 February 2002, a ceasefire came that April, and UNITA is now Angola's second-largest party.

entries_new.name: Chinese Soviet Republic
entries_new.mechanism: A party proclaimed a republic over scattered rural bases and governed them during a civil war.
entries_new.story:
The Chinese Soviet Republic was a state-within-a-state proclaimed by Chinese Communist Party leaders Mao Zedong and Zhu De on 7 November 1931, with its capital at Ruijin in Jiangxi. Its disconnected territories governed more than 3.4 million people across about 70,000 square kilometres, with Mao as chairman and prime minister.
It survived several Nationalist encirclement campaigns. A fifth, begun in 1933, used lines of fortified blockhouses. On 16 October 1934 about 130,000 soldiers and civilians broke out on the Long March. The experience helped Mao lead the Communists to victory in 1949.

entries_new.name: Hezbollah in South Lebanon
entries_new.mechanism: An armed party holds areas of a state whose parliament it sits in, and provides schools and hospitals there.
entries_new.story:
Hezbollah is a Lebanese Shia Islamist party with an armed wing. It fought Israeli forces and the South Lebanon Army through the 1980s and 1990s until Israel left southern Lebanon in 2000. It sits in Lebanon's parliament and is listed as holding South Lebanon, parts of the northeast and the Dahieh suburbs of Beirut.
It runs at least four hospitals, twelve clinics and twelve schools, along with two farm centres and a satellite TV station. On 5 August 2025 Lebanon's government announced a plan to disarm militias, and in March 2026, amid a new war, it prohibited the group's military and security activities.

entries_new.name: New People's Army barrio committees
entries_new.mechanism: A guerrilla army replaced village authority with its own committees and taxes.
entries_new.story:
The New People's Army is the armed wing of the Communist Party of the Philippines, founded on 29 March 1969. It set up barrio organising committees to cut land rent and end usury, then revolutionary committees to formally mark villages as government strongholds. By 1972 it reported 735 and 60 of these, governing an estimated 400,000 people, and it collected "revolutionary taxes" from businesses and residents.
In 2018 the party claimed to operate in 73 of the 81 provinces. In August 2025 the Philippine armed forces declared no active guerrilla fronts remained and put the group at fewer than 785 fighters.

entries_new.name: Nepal's Maoist People's Government
entries_new.mechanism: A party took over village administration in remote hill districts and then traded the war for seats in government.
entries_new.story:
The Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) fought a ten-year civil war from its base in the western hill districts of Rolpa and Rukum. By May 1998, 51 village development committees (the local government unit) in Rolpa and western Nepal were under Maoist control, running a parallel administration called the People's Government.
Chairman Prachanda signed the Comprehensive Peace Accord in 2006, ending the war. The party then entered ordinary politics and has led three national governments, in 2008, 2013 and 2016.

entries_new.name: Naxalite Red Corridor
entries_new.mechanism: Guerrilla groups held rural forest districts as a zone of influence across several Indian states.
entries_new.story:
The Naxalites are Indian communist groups who say they fight for the rural poor, in an insurgency that began after the 1967 Naxalbari uprising in West Bengal. Their zone of influence, called the Red Corridor, peaked at nearly 180 districts in the late 2000s.
It shrank to 83 districts across nine states by July 2011 and to 3 by early 2026, with over 5,000 insurgents reported killed since 2000 and more than 10,000 surrendering between 2015 and 2025. India declared victory on 30 March 2026. A writer in The Hindu said the government had extended the crackdown from jungles to cities by treating dissent as insurgency.

entries_new.name: Dáil Courts
entries_new.laws: Decree of the First Dáil, 29 June 1920
entries_new.mechanism: A rebel parliament built a court system to draw people away from the state's courts during a war.
entries_new.story:
The Dáil Courts, or Republican Courts, were the courts of the Irish Republic that declared independence in 1919, set up by decree of the Dáil parliament on 29 June 1920 to undermine British rule. Local IRA men, clergy or Sinn Féin figures sat as judges in parish courts, and women could serve. The IRA and Irish Republican Police enforced rulings, and serious offenders could be exiled.
A judge, Terence MacSwiney, was arrested at a sitting on 12 August 1920. After the Treaty, the Provisional Government abolished the courts by decree on 26 July 1922, following a dispute over a habeas corpus order, and jailed the judge who issued it.

entries_new.name: Free Derry
entries_new.mechanism: Residents barricaded their streets to keep state police out and handled crime themselves.
entries_new.story:
Free Derry was a self-declared autonomous nationalist area in the Bogside and Creggan neighbourhoods of Derry, Northern Ireland. Residents first barricaded it against the Royal Ulster Constabulary on 5 January 1969, keeping police out for six days. Barricades returned that August, with first aid posts and a radio station.
After they went up again later, unarmed auxiliaries staffed them and a voluntary Free Derry Police handled crime. On 31 July 1972, in Operation Motorman, thousands of British troops with armoured bulldozers dismantled the barricades. The IRA had decided not to resist.

entries_new.name: Khun Sa's Shan border territory
entries_new.stopped_by: US pressure on his brokers; surrender to Burma, 1996
entries_new.challenge: Thailand; Burma; US Drug Enforcement Administration
entries_new.mechanism: A militia leader sold protection to heroin refiners on a border and traded favours with the armies on both sides.
entries_new.story:
Khun Sa, born Zhang Qifu in Burma's Shan State, was the dominant opium warlord of the Golden Triangle from about 1976 to 1996. As a government-backed home guard leader from 1963, he was allowed to trade opium in return for fighting rebels. From 1985 his Mong Tai Army held a 150-mile strip of the Thai-Burma border, based at Ho Mong, with refineries whose owners paid him for protection. He commanded 20,000 men, and he may once have supplied a quarter of the world's heroin.
The US put a 2 million dollar bounty on him. Thailand drove him out in 1982, and Burma tolerated him in return for fighting rebels. In 1996 he surrendered to Burma, disbanded his army and moved to Yangon, where he ran business projects until his death in 2007.

entries_new.name: Fatahland
entries_new.challenge: Israel; Lebanese Christian militias; local Lebanese groups
entries_new.mechanism: An exiled movement took its headquarters into a neighbouring country and ran its own area there.
entries_new.story:
Fatahland was the name for the proto-state, a government without being a state, that the Palestine Liberation Organization built in South and Central Lebanon after Jordan expelled it in July 1971. Egypt had pressed Lebanon into the Cairo Agreement of 1969, which let bases open there.
The PLO allied with local leftist groups and launched attacks on the Galilee and elsewhere. Its alliance's treatment of local people turned Sunnis, Shia and Christians against it. Israel invaded South Lebanon in 1978 and again in 1982, reaching Beirut. About 8,000 PLO fighters left the city and the leadership moved to Tunis.

entries_new.name: Provisional Revolutionary Government of South Vietnam
entries_new.founder: North Vietnam and the Viet Cong
entries_new.mechanism: A rival government formed in wartime won recognition from some states and signed the peace treaty as a party.
entries_new.story:
The Provisional Revolutionary Government was formed on 8 June 1969 by North Vietnam, with delegates of the Viet Cong, as an armed rival to the South Vietnamese government under President Thiệu. Most communist states and Malta recognised it, and it signed the 1973 Paris Peace Treaty as a party separate from both Vietnams.
After Saigon fell on 30 April 1975 it became the nominal government of the Republic of South Vietnam, taking over the old government's property, rights and obligations. On 2 July 1976 the South merged into the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam

entries_new.name: Ansar al-Sharia emirates in southern Yemen
entries_new.challenge: Yemeni government; Houthi and Saleh forces; United States
entries_new.mechanism: An al-Qaeda affiliate took southern towns in a time of national upheaval and named them emirates.
entries_new.story:
Ansar al-Sharia is an umbrella group that al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula created in Yemen in 2011 to fight an insurgency at home. After the Battle of Zinjibar, between May and September 2011, it held some southern cities and declared them emirates.
The International Crisis Group described many of its members as not committed to al-Qaeda's global aims. The United States listed it in October 2012 as another name for AQAP, and the UN listed it the same day. In 2017 it was fighting Houthi and Saleh forces for territory in five governorates.

entries_new.name: Pakistani Taliban in the tribal areas
entries_new.mechanism: Armed groups established authority in a border region by fighting and negotiating with the state at once.
entries_new.story:
The Pakistani Taliban (Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, TTP) is a jihadist group on the Afghan border, designated as terrorist by the UN, Pakistan and the United States. Its roots lie in Pakistani army incursions into the tribal areas from 2002.
In 2004 the groups that later formed it effectively established their authority in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, by attacking the army while negotiating with Islamabad. Pakistan's airstrikes in Afghanistan in April 2022 appeared to respond to a rise in attacks.

entries_new.name: FMLN fronts in El Salvador
entries_new.mechanism: A guerrilla coalition held rural pockets in five fronts, then traded its army for party status.
entries_new.story:
The Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front (FMLN) merged leftist guerrilla groups on 10 October 1980 during El Salvador's civil war. Its offensive of January 1981 failed, though it kept control of some territory. It divided itself into five fronts across named departments, including a northern front in Chalatenango and an eastern front in Morazán and neighbouring areas.
The Chapultepec Peace Accords ended the war in 1992, and the FMLN demobilised and registered as a political party.

entries_new.name: RENAMO in Mozambique
entries_new.founder: Rhodesian Central Intelligence Organisation; André Matsangaissa
entries_new.mechanism: A rebel force sponsored by a neighbouring government fought from the countryside and later became an opposition party.
entries_new.story:
RENAMO, the Mozambican National Resistance, was founded in May 1977 with the active sponsorship of Rhodesian intelligence, from dissidents opposed to the ruling FRELIMO party. It fought until the Rome General Peace Accords of October 1992, which ended the one-party state and brought multi-party elections, monitored by a UN mission until 1994.
Renewed clashes between its forces and the government began in 2013. A second peace agreement in August 2019 largely ended the insurgency. RENAMO remains a political party.

entries_new.name: Bougainville Revolutionary Army rule, 1990
entries_new.challenge: Papua New Guinea; Australia; rival armed groups on the island
entries_new.mechanism: Rebels took an island when government troops withdrew, and held it under blockade.
entries_new.story:
Bougainville is an island in Papua New Guinea, home to the Panguna copper mine, which once produced more than 45% of the country's export revenue. A dispute over the mine became a separatist war in 1988. In early 1990 Papua New Guinea's forces withdrew, leaving the island to the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA), and in May 1990 its leader Francis Ona declared independence.
The government imposed a blockade until a 1994 ceasefire, continued informally in places until 1997. Estimates of the dead run from 1,000 to 2,000 up to 15,000 to 20,000. The 1998 peace deal led to an autonomous government. The later independence vote is a separate entry.

entries_new.name: Yan Xishan's Shanxi
entries_new.stopped_by: Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War
entries_new.challenge: Yuan Shikai; Japan; Chinese Communists; Nationalists in the 1930 Central Plains War
entries_new.mechanism: A provincial commander kept one province for 38 years by changing allies as each stronger power came and went.
entries_new.story:
Yan Xishan, a Chinese warlord, effectively controlled the landlocked province of Shanxi from the 1911 revolution until the Communist victory of 1949, surviving Yuan Shikai, the Warlord Era, the Nationalist period and the Japanese invasion. His alliances moved: he joined the anti-Japanese front in 1937, negotiated with Japan from 1940 to 1943 and allied with it against the Communists from 1944.
His forces at Taiyuan were a major obstacle to the Communists. He fled in 1949 and served as the last premier of the Republic of China on the mainland and its first in Taiwan.

entries_new.name: Fengtian clique in Manchuria
entries_new.mechanism: A warlord ran a region with foreign backing, protecting that foreign power's interests in return.
entries_new.story:
The Fengtian clique was the faction behind the warlord Zhang Zuolin in China's Warlord Era, based in Fengtian Province and soon controlling all three northeastern provinces. Japan backed it in exchange for protecting Japanese interests in Manchuria, and it shared or fought for control of Beijing in two wars with the Zhili clique in 1922 and 1924.
In 1928 his Japanese sponsors killed Zhang by blowing up his train. His son pledged allegiance to the Nationalist government at Nanjing, but in practice the clique went on governing Manchuria independently until Japan invaded in 1931.

entries_new.name: Long Yun's Yunnan
entries_new.stopped_by: Kunming Incident coup ordered by Chiang Kai-shek
entries_new.mechanism: A general seized a province and ran its money and tax, while holding a post under the national government.
entries_new.story:
Long Yun, an ethnic Yi commander, took power in the Chinese province of Yunnan by a coup in February 1927 against the governor Tang Jiyao, and ran it as governor and warlord until October 1945. He expanded paper money in the province, reorganised tariff taxes, measured land for a reformed tax and pushed grain farming.
He held a Nationalist Army command at the same time as his provincial office. Chiang Kai-shek ended his rule with a coup carried out by Du Yuming, known as the Kunming Incident.

zones_new.name: Rebel-run territory during a war
zones_new.who_owns: The land stays, in law, with the country it sits in. An armed movement can hold it, tax it and judge people on it, and treaties that bind the movement in the war say this changes nobody's legal status.

rules.says: In a war inside one country, no one may be sentenced or executed without judgment by a 'regularly constituted court'. Applying the article 'shall not affect the legal status of the Parties to the conflict'.
Covers wars between a state's forces and organised armed groups that control part of its territory, under responsible command.
Does not apply to riots and isolated or sporadic violence.
Nothing in the Protocol may be used to affect the sovereignty of a state or its right to restore order by lawful means.
A sentence may follow only a conviction by a court offering essential guarantees of independence and impartiality.

Sentencing without a regularly constituted court, and pillaging a town or place, are war crimes in internal armed conflicts. Art. 8(2)(f) covers protracted conflict between governments and organised armed groups, or between such groups.

zones_new.hook: Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions lets a war's rules bind a rebel movement while saying they do not change its legal status, so holding the land and running courts on it gives no title to it.
zones_new.can_you_build: Physically, armed movements have built schools, clinics, courts and tax offices on land they held, as the Karen National Union did in eastern Myanmar in the 1990s. Legally, there is no permit for this: the country whose land it is treats it as rebellion, and foreign states need not give the movement's court rulings any legal effect.
facts: Karen Albert's Rebel Quasi-State Institutions dataset covers 235 rebel groups from 1945 to 2012 and codes 25 kinds of institution. Nearly 64% created at least one governing institution.
A Wikipedia list of rebel groups that control territory, tagged as needing more citations, ran to about 43 rows when read in November 2026, 16 of them in Myanmar.
Colombia's president gave FARC a 42,000 square kilometre safe haven in 1998 and ordered it retaken in 2002.
Chinese Soviet Republic, 1931 to 1934: more than 3.4 million people across about 70,000 square kilometres.
Al-Shabaab runs named departments for tax, local administration, courts and police.
zones_new.essay:
Rebel-run territory is land where an armed movement fighting a government also acts as a government, while the war is still going on. It differs from a settled unrecognised state such as Somaliland or Wa State, listed elsewhere, because the fighting has not stopped and the line can move in any month. The owner on paper does not change. The people there pay tax to one authority, and the law of the wider world names another.

This is common. Karen Albert's dataset in the Journal of Peace Research covers 235 rebel groups from 1945 to 2012, codes 25 kinds of institution for every year, and finds that nearly 64% created at least one governing institution. Her abstract reports that rebel strength does not predict all institutions in the same direction, and that the pattern changed after the Cold War.

The forms vary. In Ireland the Dáil, the rebel parliament, decreed a court system on 29 June 1920 to undermine British rule, with local IRA men, clergy and Sinn Féin figures sitting as judges and women eligible. In Nepal, by May 1998 Maoists controlled 51 village development committees (the local government unit) and ran a parallel People's Government. In the Philippines the New People's Army reported 735 organising committees and 60 revolutionary committees by 1972, covering an estimated 400,000 people, and collected what it called revolutionary taxes. In Somalia, al-Shabaab has named departments for tax, local administration, courts and police. The researcher Ana Arjona, studying Colombia, uses the word rebelocracy for cases where an armed group regulates many parts of local life, and finds that communities with strong local institutions can limit that control.

International law addresses all this without granting anything. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions binds both sides of an internal war, forbids sentences without a regularly constituted court, and says its application does not affect the legal status of the parties. Additional Protocol II covers groups that control part of a state's territory, and says nothing in it may be used to affect that state's sovereignty. An ICRC blog post records a live argument: one view, associated with a scholar named Bhuta and Justice Alito's dissent in the US case Hamdan, reads a regular court as one set up under a state's domestic law, leaving rebels no basis for courts at all. The author argues that equality between the two sides should let an armed group rely on its own legislation, and notes that the 2016 ICRC commentary says states need not give such trials legal effect.

Endings show how the land is lost or kept. Colombia gave FARC 42,000 square kilometres in 1998 and ordered the army to retake it on 21 February 2002. The Chinese Soviet Republic governed over 3.4 million people until encirclement forced its leaders out in October 1934, and those leaders won China in 1949. Nepal's Maoists signed a peace accord in 2006 and went on to lead governments. Free Derry's barricades came down on 31 July 1972 before thousands of British troops. Each of these movements rested on a people or a party with a claim of its own, and none of them was a private venture. Where such a movement won, the result was an ordinary state or a seat in an existing government, under ordinary law.

odds.why: Estimates. Holding ground is possible with fighters and a local population, and 64% of the groups in one dataset built some institution. Law gives nothing: Common Article 3 leaves legal status unchanged. Money comes from taxing people and trade, which requires the land first. Most holdings end through defeat or a peace deal, and recognition by another state is rare.

own.own_why: You get courts, taxes and police on land while you hold it, which fails the test because the state still claims it and attacks when able. Caguán lasted about 3 years and the Chinese Soviet Republic 3. Hamas, the Houthis and al-Shabaab have passed 10 years under attack, and all of them rest on an existing people or movement, so a private group has far less to stand on.

zones_new.name: Warlords and armed crime running territory
zones_new.who_owns: The country it sits in. A warlord or armed criminal group holds the land by force and makes money from it, and may have a deal with the state's officers, but no law transfers it to them.

rules.cite: UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, Art. 2(a)
rules.says: An organised criminal group is a structured group of three or more persons, existing for a period of time and acting together to commit serious crimes for financial or other material benefit.

rules.cite: UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, Art. 5
rules.says: Each party must make it a crime to knowingly take part in such a group's criminal activities, or to organise, direct or assist serious crime involving one.
Pillaging a town or place, even when taken by assault, is a war crime in an internal armed conflict.
Required all states to prohibit the direct or indirect import of all rough diamonds from Sierra Leone.

zones_new.hook: Crime laws under a UN treaty apply to everyone who takes part in the group, so running a territory this way leaves its leaders open to arrest, sanctions, extradition or trial whenever they lose control or leave.
zones_new.can_you_build: Physically, yes while the guns and local deals hold: KK Park in Myanmar had its own supermarkets, hospital and hotels, and Greater Liberia had its own currency and airfields. Legally, nothing built this way has any standing, and Myanmar approved only 59 villas at Shwe Kokko against a project promoted as a 15 billion US dollar zone.
facts: Rio de Janeiro, 2020 study: militias held 57.5% of the city's territory and about 2.2 million residents; Comando Vermelho 11.4%.
OHCHR, 2023: at least 120,000 people in Myanmar may be held in forced online scam work, with estimates around 100,000 in Cambodia.
Kokang, Myanmar: about 1,895 square kilometres and about 150,000 people in 2009.
China's Warlord Era ran from 1916 to 1928, by the usual count.
Charles Taylor was sentenced to 50 years by the Special Court for Sierra Leone on 11 counts.
zones_new.essay:
A warlord or armed criminal group runs territory for what it pays. The aim is income from diamonds, opium, casinos, extortion or scam compounds, and any courts and services serve that income. Some of these groups also have political programmes, and the line with rebel movements is not clean. The land stays, in law, with the country around it.

The largest cases grew where a state had collapsed. After Yuan Shikai died in 1916, China split among military cliques, with Zhang Zuolin holding Manchuria and rival groups holding northern and southeastern provinces, and whoever held Beijing claimed the national government. Reunification in 1928 was partial: Yan Xishan of Shanxi rebelled in 1929 and several warlords kept influence into the 1940s. In Liberia, Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front held up to 90% of the country, ran a capital at Gbarnga with its own currency, banks and radio, and exported diamonds, timber and gold. He then won election as president. A UN-backed court later sentenced him to 50 years for aiding Sierra Leone's RUF rebels. The RUF held diamond fields and bought arms with the money, and the UN Security Council banned imports of Sierra Leone's rough diamonds on 5 July 2000.

The scam towns of Myanmar show the modern form. Shwe Kokko, on the Thai border, is the headquarters of a militia of about 6,000 troops whose company was due 30% of the profits of Yatai New City. Yatai promoted it as a 15 billion US dollar special economic zone, and Myanmar never approved one. KK Park nearby had its own hospital and hotels, and a 2024 Deutsche Welle investigation reported confiscated passports, 17-hour days and torture. The UN human rights office reported in 2023 that at least 120,000 people across Myanmar might be held in forced scam work. Pressure came from outside: Thailand cut power and fuel in February 2025 after pressure from China, and Myanmar's army raided KK Park in October 2025 and Shwe Kokko in November. Critics quoted by AP say the masterminds carry on elsewhere. The Karen groups accused of involvement deny it.

Inside working countries, armed groups can hold neighbourhoods with no claim to independence. A 2020 study of Rio de Janeiro, built from 37,883 tip-line reports, gave militias 57.5% of the city's territory and Comando Vermelho 11.4%. In Medellín, the Oficina de Envigado acted as chief mediator and debt collector in drug disputes, and its leader Diego Murillo struck a deal with authorities from prison to keep violence down before he was extradited in 2008. In Michoacán the Knights Templar Cartel fought rivals and armed residents until federal police arrested its leader in 2015; it is believed to have ended by 2017.

The record on duration is mixed. Kokang's MNDAA got a ceasefire and a self-run special region in 1989, lost it to the army after refusing to become a border guard force in 2009, and retook its capital in December 2023. In September 2025 China sentenced 16 members of a Kokang crime family to death. Holding depends on a state's attention and on neighbouring states' tolerance, and the people at the top carry personal legal risk that outlasts the territory.

odds.why: Estimates. Force and illegal income can build a compound or hold a town, and KK Park went up in about two years. Law offers nothing, and organised crime treaties make taking part an offence. Money is the strongest element, since these groups exist for it. Holding depends on neighbouring states; Thailand's power cut and Myanmar's raids ended the visible phase of KK Park in about 6 years. No recognition by another state was found for these cases.

own.own_why: You get armed control and income, and rules enforced by your own men, while a state looks away. It fails the test because the state's law still applies and can return, as at Kokang in 2009 and KK Park in 2025, and leaders face arrest abroad. Figure sits below holding land with private soldiers because the income itself draws outside enforcement.
